newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Canada to drop threats on salmon talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Canada to drop threats on salmon talks.

text.p: The United States called on Canada on Wednesday to drop threats and return to the bargaining table "in good faith" so that collapsed negotiations on Pacific salmon fishing can resume.
The United States Tuesday cancelled the next round of negotiations, scheduled for Friday, after Canadian authorities, frustrated by the slow pace of the talks, seized four American trawlers.

The State Department said Wednesday it was "very disappointed" that it had to postpone the negotiations, which an earlier statement said could not be held "until a more favourable climate for discussions can be achieved."
Spokesman John Dinger said Washington was pleased that Canada had now released three of the four trawlers after they paid small fines.

"What needs to happen now is that, one, there needs to be an end to these threats because frankly we feel that they are counter-productive, and two, we believe the Canadian negotiator needs to indicate to us that he is willing to go back to the negotiating table also in a spirit of good faith and compromise," he told reporters.
Canada and the United States have skirmished for years over salmon catches in the Pacific Northwest and pressure for a deal is mounting before this year's salmon run begins in the next few weeks.

Last week the Canadians angrily halted talks when U.S. negotiators said they were not authorised to offer a specific catch reduction at the session. Canada is concerned about overfishing by American boats as salmon head through Alaskan waters into Canadian waters to breed.
The Americans argued that U.S. "stakeholders" in the issue -- states and native tribes affected -- needed a 30-day period to consider a proposed deal.

"We felt we were 30 days, perhaps less than 30 days, away from being able to conclude a successful agreement," Dinger said. "It perplexes us that after years and years of hard negotiating an additional 30 days or less was somehow too long to wait."

Dinger said U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, travelling in Europe, hoped to speak to Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy "in the very near future to see if there's any progress she can make at her level".
